texts.154g-P13v: Now, the Zapatistas also don't prove my whole economic path. (That's the one that goes from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money.) Do their communities use collective work to support their schools and clinics, and their autonomous government and resistance? Yes. But they also sell products and trade, and they get outside support. So what they've shown is that you can stop buying major necessities and public functions on the market, and govern them collectively instead. Outside help can make a community more capable, sure. But if the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable, it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence.

texts.154g-P16b3P17p:
In my research, I also tried to follow what happened after the Escuelita. I found alumni networks, people bringing practices home, and organizing later on. What I didn't find was a clear chain from an Escuelita student to a newly founded communal institution, with evidence of how its members and their kids actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already traveling internationally before the Escuelita, so a resemblance later on doesn't prove by itself that it came from the Escuelita. I'm borrowing a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate, and I'm not claiming the Zapatistas have already proved my whole model.

Sociocracy has a very different history, but it ended up with some similar forms. It uses circles and consent, and it distributes authority and links its levels. That doesn't prove a universal formula. But builders get another serious system to study, instead of inventing governance during their first dispute.
